issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette:
Priya Sharma was twenty-eight when the building collapsed. She had been a junior policy analyst at the City Planning Department then, newly promoted and eager to prove herself on a mixed-use development project in the warehouse district. The structure was a century-old manufacturing plant being retrofitted into apartments and retail space. On a Tuesday morning in March, she was inside conducting a final inspection before the city signed off on the conversion. She was standing in the central atrium, reviewing structural diagrams with the project manager, when she heard a sound like the world cracking-a deep, spreading groan of metal and concrete giving way. The collapse took seconds. The ceiling above the eastern wing fell first, and then the failure cascaded. She ran toward the exit, her legs moving faster than her mind could process what was happening, and made it through the main doors as the structure behind her folded in on itself. Dust filled the street. She stood on the sidewalk, coughing, her hands shaking, watching emergency vehicles arrive. Three workers died in the rubble. The project manager, who had been standing two feet from her, was never found intact.

In the weeks after, Priya returned to work. She had to. The city launched an investigation; there were depositions, reviews of the engineering reports she had signed off on, questions about whether she had missed something, whether her inexperience had contributed to the deaths. She hadn't missed anything-the original structural assessment had been falsified by the contractor-but the doubt had already taken root. She came to believe that the world operated on hidden dangers, that catastrophe was always present, waiting for the moment you let your guard down. If she had been standing two feet to the left, she would have died. The randomness of it terrified her. She began having intrusive images of the moment just before the collapse, the project manager's face as he turned toward the sound, the dust cloud billowing through the atrium. These images arrived without warning-while she was eating breakfast, sitting in traffic, listening to a colleague speak-and each time they did, her body flooded with the same terror she had felt on that Tuesday morning. Her heart would race. Her hands would go cold. She would find herself holding her breath. Loud noises-a car backfiring, construction equipment, even a door slamming-would send her into a state of acute alarm, her mind immediately searching for structural failure, for collapse, for the specific acoustic signature of disaster. She found herself unable to concentrate during meetings; her attention would fragment, pulled toward environmental monitoring. She had difficulty falling asleep and, when she did sleep, her dreams were saturated with the sensation of falling, of being buried, of not being able to breathe. She would wake gasping, her clothes soaked with sweat, her heart hammering against her ribs.

Four years later, at thirty-two, Priya is a City Council Member, elected on a platform of infrastructure safety and accountability. Her colleagues describe her as meticulous, thorough, relentless in her questioning of contractors and engineers. What they don't see is the machinery running underneath. Every morning before dawn, Priya lies awake, her mind cycling through the day ahead-the meetings, the people, the spaces she will move through. She has come to believe that she must be on guard all the time, that constant vigilance is the only thing standing between herself and another catastrophe. At night, the city feels different to her. The darkness makes her uncertain about what is happening around her, and she finds it harder to feel safe. She keeps her bedroom door open so she can hear if something is wrong. She sleeps poorly, waking several times in the night with a surge of dread, her mind searching for the threat that has jolted her awake even though there is nothing there. The sleep disruption has accumulated over years now; she moves through her days on a foundation of exhaustion that no amount of coffee can quite remedy, and she has begun to notice that her concentration slips in afternoon meetings, that her patience with staff has worn thin. She has also developed a tremor in her hands that appears without warning-when she is holding a pen during a council session, when she is signing legislation, when she is simply sitting still. The tremor embarrasses her. She has learned to grip her hands together or to clasp them in her lap during public appearances, a posture that has become so habitual that her staff assumes it is simply how she sits.

When she enters a building for a council meeting or a site visit, she identifies the exits before she sits down. She knows the stairs, the side doors, the windows that open onto fire escapes. In unfamiliar places-a new restaurant, a conference venue, a colleague's home-she avoids going altogether. She cannot assess the danger in spaces she hasn't mapped, and the anxiety of not knowing is worse than the disappointment of declining the invitation. Her social life has narrowed. She hasn't been on a date in three years. The thought of being in someone else's apartment, in a space she doesn't control, where she can't identify escape routes, is unbearable. She is hypervigilant toward people-watching faces, postures, the way someone holds their hands-trying to spot danger before it manifests. She scans every environment she enters, a habit so automatic now that she barely notices she is doing it. She has also systematically eliminated anything that puts her body under physical stress. She stopped running six months ago; the elevated heart rate felt too close to panic, and she couldn't distinguish between her body's normal response to exertion and the beginning of a threat response. She quit the gym. She stopped attending the yoga classes her doctor recommended. Last month, when a colleague invited her to play recreational tennis-something she had enjoyed in college-she declined without explanation. The thought of her heart racing, her breathing quickening, her body in a state of arousal, was intolerable. She takes the elevator instead of the stairs, avoiding the exertion. She has even stopped walking briskly; a slow, controlled pace through the world feels safer, more manageable. Any situation that might elevate her physical state-climbing, lifting, sustained movement-has become something she structures her day to avoid. The logic is clear to her: if her body is calm, if her heart rate stays steady and low, then she can monitor her internal state clearly, and she will know if real danger is approaching.

Three weeks ago, during a particularly tense budget meeting, a contractor raised his voice in disagreement with her. He wasn't angry at her specifically; he was frustrated with the process. But Priya felt her body flood with fear. Her hands trembled visibly. She excused herself and went to her office, where she sat in the dark for an hour, certain that something terrible was about to happen. That night, she couldn't sleep. The next morning, she called a therapist. She is afraid that this vigilance, this constant bracing for disaster, is the only thing keeping her alive-and she is exhausted. She wants to feel safe again, but she is terrified of what might happen if she stops watching, if she allows her body to move naturally, if she relaxes her grip on the world even for a moment. What frightens her most is not the possibility of another collapse, though that fear runs deep. It is the fear that if she lets go of her vigilance, if she stops scanning, stops planning, stops monitoring her own body for signs of threat, then she will miss the warning signs and someone will die because of her carelessness. She carries the weight of the three workers and the project manager as a kind of proof that her fear is rational, that the world is genuinely dangerous, and that she alone must stand guard against it.

She wants to feel safe again, but she is terrified of what might happen if she stops watching, if she allows her body to move naturally, if she relaxes her grip on the world even for a moment.

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Priya Sharma was twenty-eight when the building collapsed. She had been a junior policy analyst at the City Planning Department then, newly promoted and eager to prove herself on a mixed-use development project in the warehouse district. The structure was a century-old manufacturing plant being retrofitted into apartments and retail space. On a Tuesday morning in March, she was inside conducting a final inspection before the city signed off on the conversion. She was standing in the central atrium, reviewing structural diagrams with the project manager, when she heard a sound like the world cracking—a deep, spreading groan of metal and concrete giving way. The collapse took seconds. The ceiling above the eastern wing fell first, and then the failure cascaded. She ran toward the exit, her legs moving faster than her mind could process what was happening, and made it through the main doors as the structure behind her folded in on itself. Dust filled the street. She stood on the sidewalk, coughing, her hands shaking, watching emergency vehicles arrive. Three workers died in the rubble. The project manager, who had been standing two feet from her, was never found intact.

In the weeks after, Priya returned to work. She had to. The city launched an investigation; there were depositions, reviews of the engineering reports she had signed off on, questions about whether she had missed something, whether her inexperience had contributed to the deaths. She hadn't missed anything—the original structural assessment had been falsified by the contractor—but the doubt had already taken root. She came to believe that the world operated on hidden dangers, that catastrophe was always present, waiting for the moment you let your guard down. If she had been standing two feet to the left, she would have died. The randomness of it terrified her. She began having intrusive images of the moment just before the collapse, the project manager's face as he turned toward the sound, the dust cloud billowing through the atrium. These images arrived without warning—while she was eating breakfast, sitting in traffic, listening to a colleague speak—and each time they did, her body flooded with the same terror she had felt on that Tuesday morning. Her heart would race. Her hands would go cold. She would find herself holding her breath. Loud noises—a car backfiring, construction equipment, even a door slamming—would send her into a state of acute alarm, her mind immediately searching for structural failure, for collapse, for the specific acoustic signature of disaster. She found herself unable to concentrate during meetings; her attention would fragment, pulled toward environmental monitoring. She had difficulty falling asleep and, when she did sleep, her dreams were saturated with the sensation of falling, of being buried, of not being able to breathe. She would wake gasping, her clothes soaked with sweat, her heart hammering against her ribs.

Four years later, at thirty-two, Priya is a City Council Member, elected on a platform of infrastructure safety and accountability. Her colleagues describe her as meticulous, thorough, relentless in her questioning of contractors and engineers. What they don't see is the machinery running underneath. Every morning before dawn, Priya lies awake, her mind cycling through the day ahead—the meetings, the people, the spaces she will move through. She has come to believe that she must be on guard all the time, that constant vigilance is the only thing standing between herself and another catastrophe. At night, the city feels different to her. The darkness makes her uncertain about what is happening around her, and she finds it harder to feel safe. She keeps her bedroom door open so she can hear if something is wrong. She sleeps poorly, waking several times in the night with a surge of dread, her mind searching for the threat that has jolted her awake even though there is nothing there. The sleep disruption has accumulated over years now; she moves through her days on a foundation of exhaustion that no amount of coffee can quite remedy, and she has begun to notice that her concentration slips in afternoon meetings, that her patience with staff has worn thin. She has also developed a tremor in her hands that appears without warning—when she is holding a pen during a council session, when she is signing legislation, when she is simply sitting still. The tremor embarrasses her. She has learned to grip her hands together or to clasp them in her lap during public appearances, a posture that has become so habitual that her staff assumes it is simply how she sits.

When she enters a building for a council meeting or a site visit, she identifies the exits before she sits down. She knows the stairs, the side doors, the windows that open onto fire escapes. In unfamiliar places—a new restaurant, a conference venue, a colleague's home—she avoids going altogether. She cannot assess the danger in spaces she hasn't mapped, and the anxiety of not knowing is worse than the disappointment of declining the invitation. Her social life has narrowed. She hasn't been on a date in three years. The thought of being in someone else's apartment, in a space she doesn't control, where she can't identify escape routes, is unbearable. She is hypervigilant toward people—watching faces, postures, the way someone holds their hands—trying to spot danger before it manifests. She scans every environment she enters, a habit so automatic now that she barely notices she is doing it. She has also systematically eliminated anything that puts her body under physical stress. She stopped running six months ago; the elevated heart rate felt too close to panic, and she couldn't distinguish between her body's normal response to exertion and the beginning of a threat response. She quit the gym. She stopped attending the yoga classes her doctor recommended. Last month, when a colleague invited her to play recreational tennis—something she had enjoyed in college—she declined without explanation. The thought of her heart racing, her breathing quickening, her body in a state of arousal, was intolerable. She takes the elevator instead of the stairs, avoiding the exertion. She has even stopped walking briskly; a slow, controlled pace through the world feels safer, more manageable. Any situation that might elevate her physical state—climbing, lifting, sustained movement—has become something she structures her day to avoid. The logic is clear to her: if her body is calm, if her heart rate stays steady and low, then she can monitor her internal state clearly, and she will know if real danger is approaching.

Three weeks ago, during a particularly tense budget meeting, a contractor raised his voice in disagreement with her. He wasn't angry at her specifically; he was frustrated with the process. But Priya felt her body flood with fear. Her hands trembled visibly. She excused herself and went to her office, where she sat in the dark for an hour, certain that something terrible was about to happen. That night, she couldn't sleep. The next morning, she called a therapist. She is afraid that this vigilance, this constant bracing for disaster, is the only thing keeping her alive—and she is exhausted. She wants to feel safe again, but she is terrified of what might happen if she stops watching, if she allows her body to move naturally, if she relaxes her grip on the world even for a moment. What frightens her most is not the possibility of another collapse, though that fear runs deep. It is the fear that if she lets go of her vigilance, if she stops scanning, stops planning, stops monitoring her own body for signs of threat, then she will miss the warning signs and someone will die because of her carelessness. She carries the weight of the three workers and the project manager as a kind of proof that her fear is rational, that the world is genuinely dangerous, and that she alone must stand guard against it.
